name: Retroclined incisor theory

lead: Retroclined incisor theory is a discussion topic in looksmaxxing forums about the tilt of the front teeth. Retroclined incisors lean back toward the throat; proclined ones lean forward. Proponents argue that the angle of the incisors shapes lip support, the lower-face profile and even how the chin appears.

Orthodontists treat incisor position as one factor in lip posture and profile, and a perception study found profile views with the upper incisor slightly retroclined (about 85 degrees) rated most attractive.

paras: In forum discussion, people compare their incisor inclination in profile photos or X-rays and discuss orthodontic options. One thread mentions bite and tongue or lip posture experiments alongside alveolar compensation. Actual tooth-angle changes are made by orthodontists using braces or aligners.

Moving teeth changes the bite and the lips, and over-retraction or over-proclination can worsen a profile. Orthodontic treatment carries standard risks such as root resorption and relapse, and bite-based DIY experiments reported in forums can injure cheeks and gums.

angle.text: The theory holds that incisor inclination changes how the lips and lower face sit in profile. People use it to evaluate their own teeth angle and to frame questions for an orthodontist.

lead: Retroclined incisor theory is an informal framework discussed on looksmaxxing forums, centred on the inclination of the upper and lower front teeth and its effect on facial profile. A retroclined incisor tilts toward the tongue; a proclined incisor tilts toward the lip. Posters link the angle to lip support, the look of the lower face and how prominent the chin appears [1].

Orthodontic practice treats incisor position as one factor in lip support and soft-tissue profile. Retroclined upper central incisors are also the defining feature of Class II division 2 malocclusion [2].

A 2019 perception study ranked profile images of an idealised female face with the maxillary incisor angle varied from 70 to 120 degrees; the most attractive angle was 85 degrees, about 5 degrees retroclined from vertical, and most observers recommended treatment beyond about 105 degrees [3].
infobox: Upper incisor about 85 degrees rated most attractive in one study [3]

paras: Incisor inclination is measured in profile as the angle of the labial face of the upper incisor against the vertical, and orthodontists treat it as one factor in lip posture and profile.

A looksmax.org thread titled as saying a creator referred to as Mike Jew had confirmed the theory shows the kind of discussion: one poster says an orthodontist left them with forward-inclined incisors, and another speculates about a 'butterfly bite', slight jutting and lower-lip suction as a way to influence chin position, while noting that it sucked their cheek into the gap and led to a bitten cheek [1]. The thread also mentions alveolar compensation [1].

The 2019 perception study used a single idealised female image, so its results may not generalise to other faces [3]. Wikipedia notes that orthodontic trials do not recommend any particular approach for Class II division 2 [2].
No studies found testing the community theory itself. Orthodontic research on incisor inclination and lip profile exists, including a 2019 perception study of idealised profiles [3].

lore.intro: The theory circulates in looksmax.org threads that mix orthodontic terms with bite and posture experiments [1].
